about: The lessons' support-language text: lesson.<id>.title, .text, .summary, .objective; each step's lesson.<id>.<step>.text, .translation, .help, .retry, .personRetry, .tenseRetry, .presentNote, .hud and .option.<n>.

strings.lesson.first-words.title: First words with {npc:guide}
strings.lesson.first-words.text: Seven short units: hello, yes and no, what is this, please and thank you, I and you with three verbs, getting unstuck, and what the camp needs.
strings.lesson.first-words.summary: You can greet, say yes and no, ask what something is, be polite, and say what you want, have and need.
strings.lesson.first-words.u1-welcome.text: This is {npc:guide}, the guide. She teaches you Spanish one phrase at a time. Nothing here is a test. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
strings.lesson.first-words.u1-say-hola.text: Say hello back: “Hola” (OH-lah). Hold {key:listen} to speak into the microphone, or press W to type.
strings.lesson.first-words.u1-say-hola.help: Say: Hola (OH-lah). It means hello. The letter h is silent in Spanish.
strings.lesson.first-words.u1-say-hola.retry: Not quite. Say: Hola. It means hello.
strings.lesson.first-words.u1-name.text: {npc:guide} tells you her name. “Me llamo” means “my name is”. You only need to understand this one, not say it.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-intro.text: Next: yes and no. {npc:guide} holds things up and asks about them. Answer “Sí” for yes or “No” for no.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-ask-wood.text: {npc:guide} holds up a log of wood and asks if it is wood. “Madera” means wood.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-yes.text: It is wood, so the answer is yes. Say “Sí” (SEE).
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-yes.help: Say: Sí (SEE). It means yes. It is written sí, with an accent; si without the accent means “if”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-yes.retry: Not quite. It is wood, so say: Sí.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-no.text: She holds up the same log and asks if it is water. It is not: answer “No”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u2-no.retry: Not quite. A log is not water, so say: No.
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-intro.text: Now ask what things are. “¿Qué es esto?” means “What is this?”. {npc:guide} points at something and names it.
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-ask-1.text: {npc:guide} points at a log. Ask her: “¿Qué es esto?” (keh ehs EHS-toh).
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-ask-1.help: Say: ¿Qué es esto? It means what is this?
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-ask-2.text: {npc:guide} points at some fruit. Ask again.
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-is-2.text: “Una fruta” is “a fruit”: una means a. Madera and agua need no una, just like wood and water in English.
strings.lesson.first-words.u3-ask-3.text: {npc:guide} holds up a bottle of water.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-intro.text: Good manners. When someone offers you something, “Sí, por favor” means “yes, please”, and “Gracias” means “thank you”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-offer.text: {npc:guide} offers you some fruit. “¿Quieres…?” means “do you want…?”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-yes.text: You would like some. Say: “Sí, por favor” (SEE, por fah-VOR).
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-yes.help: Say: Sí, por favor. It means yes, please.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-yes.retry: Not quite. Say: Sí, por favor.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-take.text: {npc:guide} nods at the berry bushes. You pick the fruit yourself.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-pick.text: Press Esc to close this panel. Aim the dot at a berry bush (the arrow shows one) and hold the left mouse button to pick a fruit. Then walk back to {npc:guide} and press E.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-pick.help: A berry bush is a green bush with red berries. Hold the left mouse button until the fruit drops into your bar.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-pick.hud: Pick a fruit from a berry bush, then go back to {npc:guide}
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-thanks.text: You have the fruit. Thank {npc:guide}: say “Gracias” (GRAH-see-ahs).
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-thanks.translation: Very good! You have a fruit.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-thanks.help: Say: Gracias. It means thank you.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-thanks.retry: Not quite. Say: Gracias. It means thank you.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4-welcome.text: “De nada” is the polite answer to “gracias”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-intro.text: Spanish verbs change their ending for who does them. For “I” (yo) the ending is -o; for “you” (tú) it is -as or -es: “quiero” is “I want”, “quieres” is “you want”. Some verbs also change in the middle: “tienes” (you have), but “tengo” (I have). {npc:guide} asks about you; answer about yourself, with -o.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-want.text: {npc:guide} asks what you want. “Quieres” is “you want”: the ending -es is for you.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-say-want.text: You want wood. Say it: “Quiero madera” (kee-EH-roh mah-DEH-rah). “Quiero” is “I want”: the ending -o is for I.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-say-want.help: Say: Quiero madera. It means I want wood.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-say-want.personRe: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-have.text: {npc:guide} asks if you have a fruit: “tienes” is “you have”. You do: say “Tengo una fruta”. Tener changes in the middle: tienes, but tengo.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-have.help: Say: Tengo una fruta. It means I have a fruit. Tengo is I have; tienes is you have.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-have.retry: Not quite. Say: Tengo una fruta.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-have.personRe: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-need.text: Now she asks what you need. Answer about yourself, with the -o ending: “Necesito agua”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-need.help: Say: Necesito agua. It means I need water.
strings.lesson.first-words.u4v-ask-need.personRe: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-intro.text: Everyone gets stuck. Three phrases help: “No sé” (I don't know), “Otra vez, por favor” (again, please) and “Más despacio, por favor” (more slowly, please). The buttons R, S and N do the same.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-quiz.text: {npc:guide} points at something new. You don't know the word yet, so say “No sé” (noh SEH). It is never wrong.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-quiz.help: Say: No sé. It means I don't know.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-quiz.retry: Say: No sé. It means I don't know.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-answer.text: When you say “No sé”, {npc:guide} tells you the answer.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-fast.text: {npc:guide} says something longer. Did you catch it?
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-fast.translation: Look. The wood is for the torch.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-again.text: Ask her to say it again: “Otra vez, por favor” (OH-trah behs, por fah-VOR). She will repeat her last line.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-again.help: Say: Otra vez, por favor. It means again, please.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-again.retry: Not quite. Say: Otra vez, por favor.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-slow.text: Now ask for it more slowly: “Más despacio, por favor” (mahs dehs-PAH-syoh). She will say it slowly.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-slow.help: Say: Más despacio, por favor. It means more slowly, please.
strings.lesson.first-words.u5-slow.retry: Not quite. Say: Más despacio, por favor.
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-task.text: {npc:guide} explains what the camp needs. What does she say?
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-task.help: “Necesitas” is “you need”. “Madera” is wood and “frutas” is fruit.
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-task.retry: Not quite. Listen again: madera and frutas.
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-task.option.3: You need a torch and a bottle.
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-explain.text: Your list is at the top right. Hold the left mouse button on trees and bushes to collect wood and fruit, make a torch at the workbench (press E) and set it on the fire ring. The village has water.
strings.lesson.first-words.u6-recap.text: You can already say or understand all of this.
strings.lesson.personas.title: Personas: he, she, we, they
strings.lesson.personas.text: Session 2: the verbs for he, she, you (polite), we, you all and they, with the villager and the shopkeeper.
strings.lesson.personas.summary: You can say what she wants and what we need or want, and you know he, she, we and they.
strings.lesson.personas.objective: Session 2: go to the village and talk to the villager to start the lesson “Personas”
strings.lesson.personas.p0-hello.text: The villager greets you. Greet him back, as you learned with {npc:guide}.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-intro.text: Session 2: more people. You know “I” (yo) and “you” (tú). Now: he or she (él, ella), we (nosotros) and they (ellos). The verb ending changes with the person. First a reminder from last time: “Quiero madera” (I want wood). The villager helps first, then you talk to the shopkeeper at the stall. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-recall.text: He asks you what you want, with “tú” as {npc:guide} did. Answer about yourself.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-recall.help: Say: Quiero madera. It means I want wood. Quieres is you want; quiero is I want.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-recall.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-she-is.text: The villager is talking about {npc:guide}. “Ella” is “she” and “es” is “is”.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-she-is.translation: Luna is the guide. She is my friend.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-ask-luna.text: He asks what {npc:guide} wants. “Quiere” is “he or she wants”. For he or she the ending is -e or -a (quiere, necesita), with no -s.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-say-she.text: Say what she wants: “Ella quiere fruta” (EH-yah kee-EH-reh FROO-tah).
strings.lesson.personas.p1-say-she.help: Say: Ella quiere fruta. It means she wants fruit. Ella is she, so quiere ends in -e.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-say-she.retry: Not quite. Say: Ella quiere fruta.
strings.lesson.personas.p1-say-she.personRetry: Say it about her: the ending -e, like “quiere”, with no -s.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-intro.text: Now “we”: nosotros. The ending is -amos or -emos: necesitamos (we need), queremos (we want), tenemos (we have). No -ie- for we: quiero, but queremos.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-go.text: “Vamos” is “we go” (the verb ir, which does not follow the pattern). Said alone, it means “let's go”. He wants to go to the stall with you.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-ask-we.text: On the way, he asks what the two of you need. Water is on your list. Answer with “we”: “Necesitamos agua”.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-ask-we.help: Say: Necesitamos agua. It means we need water.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-ask-we.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: the ending -amos or -emos, like “necesitamos”, “queremos”.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-they.text: He points at the houses of the village. Now “they”: ellos. The ending is -an or -en: tienen (they have). What does he say?
strings.lesson.personas.p2-they.help: “Ellos” is they, and “tienen” is they have.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-they.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ellos tienen.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-be.text: “Somos” is “we are”: tú y yo (you and I) make nosotros. Somos is from ser, “to be”, which does not follow the pattern.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-where.text: Where is {npc:guide}? “Está” is “is” (estar), as in “¿Dónde está el río?”. Estar is “to be” for where someone is; ser (es, somos) is for what someone is. What does he say?
strings.lesson.personas.p2-where.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ella está.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-walk.text: Press Esc to close this panel. Walk to the stall (the arrow shows it) and press {key:talk} to talk to the shopkeeper.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-walk.help: The stall is the one with the red and white awning in the village.
strings.lesson.personas.p2-walk.hud: Walk to the stall and talk to the shopkeeper
strings.lesson.personas.p3-intro.text: The shopkeeper says “usted”: the polite “you”, for someone you do not know well. Its verb ends like he or she: “necesita”, “tiene”. You still answer about yourself, with the -o of “yo”: “Necesito pan” and “Tengo una botella”. Many shopkeepers say “usted” to customers; he said “tú” last time, and both are normal.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-need.text: He asks what you need. Answer about yourself.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-need.help: Say: Necesito pan. It means I need bread.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-need.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-bottle.text: He asks if you have a bottle. Say you do.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-bottle.help: Say: Tengo una botella. It means I have a bottle.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-bottle.retry: Not quite. Say: Tengo una botella.
strings.lesson.personas.p3-bottle.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-all.text: Now he speaks to you and the villager together: “ustedes”, “you” for more than one person. In Latin America it is the only plural “you”, for friends and strangers alike. The ending is -en, like ellos: quieren.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-say-we.text: Answer for the two of you: “Queremos pan” (keh-REH-mohs pahn).
strings.lesson.personas.p4-say-we.help: Say: Queremos pan. It means we want bread.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-say-we.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: the ending -amos or -emos, like “necesitamos”, “queremos”.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-they.text: And the people of the village? “Ellos quieren” is “they want”: -en again. What does he say?
strings.lesson.personas.p4-they.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ellos quieren.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-review.text: Before you go, he asks something you have answered before. Answer him.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-table.text: Your new forms. querer: quiere, queremos, quieren. tener: tiene, tenemos, tienen. necesitar: necesita, necesitamos. ser: es, somos. estar: está. ir: vamos. Usted takes the he or she form; ustedes takes the they form. The book keeps them.
strings.lesson.personas.p4-recap.text: You can now say what she wants, what we need and what we want, and you understand he, she, you (polite), we and they.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.title: Ayer y mañana: yesterday and tomorrow
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.text: Session 3: tomorrow with ir a and an infinitive, and a few past forms, with the villager and the shopkeeper.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.summary: You can say what you are going to eat or do tomorrow, and what you ate, drank and where you went yesterday.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.objective: Session 3: go to the village and talk to the villager to start the lesson “Ayer y mañana”
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f0-review.text: First a question from last time. Answer him about yourself or about the two of you.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f0-intro.text: Session 3: yesterday and tomorrow. Three little words: ayer (yesterday), hoy (today) and mañana (tomorrow). First the verb ir, “to go”, and then “ir a” plus a verb, which is how you say what you are going to do. After that, a few past forms at the stall. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-ir.text: The verb ir, “to go”, does not follow the pattern. I go: voy. You go: vas. He, she, you (polite): va. We go: vamos. They, you all: van. “A” after it is “to”: voy a la tienda is “I go to the shop”. A and el join into al: voy al río.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.text: The villager says what you do today. Which one is it?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.translati: Today you are going to the shop.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.help: “Vas” is “you go” or “you are going”: the -s is for tú.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.option.1: You are going to the shop today.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.option.2: I am going to the shop today.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f1-you-go.option.3: We are going to the shop today.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-intro.text: Now plans: later today or tomorrow. Like English “going to”: a form of ir, then “a”, then the verb as it is in the dictionary, ending in -ar, -er or -ir (the infinitive). Voy a comer is “I am going to eat”; vamos a comer is “we are going to eat”. A place after “a” is where you go (voy a la tienda); a verb after “a” is what you are going to do. Not “voy a como” (como is “I eat”). “Mañana” can go in front: mañana voy a comer pan.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.text: He asks what you will eat tomorrow. Answer about yourself, with “voy a”: “Voy a comer pan”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.translation: What are you going to eat tomorrow?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.help: Say: Voy a comer pan. It means I am going to eat bread.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.retry: Not quite. Say: Voy a comer pan.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.personRetry: Say it about yourself: “voy a”, like “voy”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.tenseRetry: For a plan, use voy, then “a”, then the infinitive: “voy a comer”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-ask.presentNote: That is right too. Here we practise “voy a comer”: Voy a comer pan.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.text: Now he asks about the two of you. Answer with “vamos a”: “Vamos a comer fruta”. Said as a suggestion, vamos a comer also means “let's eat”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.translation: What are we going to eat?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.help: Say: Vamos a comer fruta. It means we are going to eat fruit.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.retry: Not quite. Say: Vamos a comer fruta.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: “vamos a comer”, like “vamos”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.tenseRetry: For a plan, use vamos, then “a”, then the infinitive: “vamos a comer”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-we.presentNote: That is right too. Here we practise “vamos a comer”: Vamos a comer fruta.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.text: He points at the houses. “Van a comer” is “they are going to eat”. What does he say?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.translation: They are going to eat bread.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.help: “Van a comer”: ir, a and an infinitive.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.retry: Not quite. Listen again: van a comer.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.option.1: They are going to eat bread.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f2-they.option.3: We are going to eat bread.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f3-walk.text: Press Esc to close this panel. Walk to the stall (the arrow shows it) and press {key:talk} to talk to the shopkeeper. He will ask about yesterday.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f3-walk.help: The stall is the one with the red and white awning in the village.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.f3-walk.hud: Walk to the stall and talk to the shopkeeper
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y0-review.text: The shopkeeper asks a question from last time. Answer him.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y0-intro.text: Now yesterday: ayer. Something that is over uses another form, the past. First comer: I ate is comí, you ate is comiste. With “ayer” use the past, not “ayer como” or “ayer voy”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-model.text: He tells you what he ate. “Comí” is “I ate” (comer). In the past, -í is for “I” and -iste is for “you”: comí, comiste.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-ate.text: He asks what you ate yesterday. Answer about yourself, in the past: “Ayer comí fruta”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-ate.help: Say: Ayer comí fruta. It means yesterday I ate fruit.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-ate.retry: Not quite. Say: Ayer comí fruta.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-ate.personRetry: Say it about yourself: the ending -í, like “comí”, not “comiste”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y1-ate.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past form: “comí” (I ate), not “como” or “voy a comer”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-ask.text: He asks if you went to the river. “Fuiste” is “you went”: the past of ir, which does not follow the pattern. For “I” it is “fui”. It still ends in -iste for “you”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-ask.translation: Did you go to the river yesterday?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-went.text: Say that you went: “Ayer fui al río” (ah-YEHR fwee ahl REE-oh).
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-went.help: Say: Ayer fui al río. It means yesterday I went to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-went.retry: Not quite. Say: Ayer fui al río.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y2-went.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past: “fui” (I went), not “voy”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.text: Now a form for “you”. What does he say?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.translation: Yesterday you went to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ayer fuiste.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.option.1: Yesterday you went to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.option.2: Yesterday I went to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y4-you.option.3: Tomorrow you are going to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y3-had.text: He asks if you drank water yesterday. Say you did: “Ayer bebí agua”. Beber is “to drink”, and it works like comer: bebí, bebiste.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y3-had.help: Say: Ayer bebí agua. It means yesterday I drank water.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y3-had.retry: Say the whole sentence, in the past: Ayer bebí agua.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y3-had.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past: “bebí” (I drank), not “bebo”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y5-contrast.text: Yesterday and tomorrow side by side. “Ayer fui al río” has a past form, “I went”. “Mañana voy a ir al río” has voy a and the infinitive, “I am going to go”. The usual slip is to mix them: “mañana fui” or “ayer voy”. The game will tell you.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.text: Last question: tomorrow. Say you are going to go to the river. Not “fui”: that was yesterday.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.transla: What are you going to do tomorrow?
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.help: Say: Mañana voy a ir al río. It means tomorrow I am going to go to the river.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.retry: Not quite. Say: Mañana voy a ir al río.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.personR: Say it about yourself: “voy a”, like “voy”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.tenseRe: Tomorrow uses “voy a” and the infinitive: “voy a ir”, not “fui”.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y6-tomorrow.present: That is right too. Here we practise “voy a ir”: Mañana voy a ir al río.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y7-table.text: Your new forms. ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Plans: voy a comer, vamos a comer, van a comer, voy a ir. Yesterday: comí, comiste; bebí, bebiste; fui, fuiste. Fui is also the past of ser (“I was”); here it means “I went”. The book keeps them.
strings.lesson.ayer-y-manana.y8-recap.text: You can now say what you are going to eat or do tomorrow, and what you ate, drank and where you went yesterday. Hoy is today.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.title: El pueblo: the village
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.text: Session 4: places and the way to them, with {npc:fisher} the fisher at the bridge and the villager: ¿Dónde está…?, cerca and lejos, hay, and your own walk told now, as a plan and once it is over.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.summary: You can ask where a place is and if it is far, ask if there is something, and say where you are going, what you are going to do there and where you went.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.objective: Session 4: walk down the road to the bridge and talk to {npc:fisher}, the fisher, to start the lesson “El pueblo”
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v0-hello.text: {npc:fisher} the fisher greets you. Greet him back, as you learned with {npc:guide}.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v0-intro.text: Session 4: the village. {npc:fisher} fishes by the bridge and knows every place. You ask him the way, walk there, and come back to tell him where you went. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-bakery.text: He asks what you are looking for. Ask where the bakery is: “¿Dónde está la panadería?” ¿Dónde está…? works for any place, with el or la: la panadería ends in -a.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-bakery.help: Say: ¿Dónde está la panadería? It means where is the bakery?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-bakery.retry: Not quite. Say: ¿Dónde está la panadería?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.text: Izquierda is left and derecha is right. Which does he say?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.translation: In the village, look at the tower. The bakery is on the left.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.help: “A la izquierda” is “on the left”; “a la derecha” is “on the right”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.retry: Not quite. Listen again: a la izquierda.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.option.1: The bakery is left of the tower.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.option.2: The bakery is right of the tower.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-left.option.3: The bakery is next to the river.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-smithy.text: He asks if you want anything else. Ask for the smithy the same way: “¿Dónde está la herrería?”
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-smithy.help: Say: ¿Dónde está la herrería? It means where is the smithy?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-smithy.retry: Not quite. Say: ¿Dónde está la herrería?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-right.text: The smithy is on the other side of the tower: a la derecha, on the right.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v1-right.translation: And the smithy is on the right.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-far.text: Ask if it is far: “¿Está lejos?” Lejos is far and cerca is near. Where things are takes estar: está lejos, not “es lejos”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-far.help: Say: ¿Está lejos? It means is it far?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-near.translation: No, it is near. The mountain is far.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-near.retry: Not quite. Listen again: está cerca.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-near.option.1: No, it is near. The mountain is far.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-near.option.2: Yes, it is far. The mountain is near.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v2-near.option.3: No, it is far. The mountain is near.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.text: Hay is “there is” or “there are”. What is in the village?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.translation: In the village there is a shop, a bakery and three houses.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.help: “Hay” is there is or there are; “tres casas” is three houses.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.retry: Not quite. Listen again: tres casas.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.option.1: A shop, a bakery and three houses.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.option.2: A shop, a bakery and two houses.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-houses.option.3: A bakery, a smithy and a well.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-well.text: He did not name a well. Ask if there is one: “¿Hay un pozo en el pueblo?” Pozo is masculine: un pozo.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-well.help: Say: ¿Hay un pozo en el pueblo? It means is there a well in the village?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v3-well.retry: Not quite. Say: ¿Hay un pozo en el pueblo?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-going.text: Now your walk, in three times. Voy a and a place is where you are going now: voy a la panadería. He asks where you are going: “Voy a la panadería”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-going.help: Say: Voy a la panadería. It means I am going to the bakery.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-going.retry: Not quite. Say: Voy a la panadería.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-going.tenseRetry: You are going now: “voy” (I go), not “fui”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.text: Voy a and a verb is a plan, as in session 3 (voy a comer). He asks what you are going to do there. Comprar is to buy: “Voy a comprar pan”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.translation: What are you going to do there?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.help: Say: Voy a comprar pan. It means I am going to buy bread.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.retry: Not quite. Say: Voy a comprar pan.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.personRetry: Say it about yourself: “voy a comprar”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.tenseRetry: For a plan, use voy, then “a”, then the infinitive: “voy a comprar”, not “compro”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v4-plan.presentNote: That is right too. Here we practise “voy a comprar”: Voy a comprar pan.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-bakery.text: Press Esc to close this panel and follow the arrow to the bakery (la panadería), left of the tower.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-bakery.help: Follow the road into the village; the bakery is the timber house with the oven by its wall.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-smithy.text: Now the smithy (la herrería), on the other side of the tower. Follow the arrow.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-smithy.help: The smithy is the house with the fire outside its door, right of the tower.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-villager.text: Now go to the villager in the square and press {key:talk} to talk to him.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-villager.help: The villager stands in the square, south of the tower.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v5-villager.hud: Talk to the villager in the square
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.text: He reads the signpost. “Dice” is “it says”. What does it say?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.translation: The sign says: shop, river, mountain.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.help: “El letrero” is the sign and “dice” is says.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.retry: Not quite. Listen again: tienda, río, montaña.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.option.1: The sign says: shop, river, mountain.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.option.2: The sign says: bakery, smithy, well.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-sign.option.3: The shop is next to the river.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-back.text: Press Esc and go back to {npc:fisher} at the bridge (the arrow shows it). Press {key:talk} to talk to him.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-back.help: Follow the road out of the village, west, to the bridge.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v6-back.hud: Go back to {npc:fisher} at the bridge
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-went.text: He asks if you went to the bakery. You did, and it is over: say “Sí” and the past, “Sí, fui a la panadería” (fui: I went, as in session 3).
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-went.translation: Did you go to the bakery?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-went.help: Say: Sí, fui a la panadería. It means yes, I went to the bakery.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-went.retry: Not quite. Say: Sí, fui a la panadería.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-went.tenseRetry: That walk is over: use the past, “fui” (I went), not “voy”.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-hungry.text: {npc:fisher} is hungry. Bring him three fruits from the bushes at {npc:guide}'s camp and walk up to him: he pays you two coins. It can wait; the objective line keeps it.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v7-hungry.translation: I am hungry. Do you have any fruit?
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v8-thanks.text: He says you know the village now. Thank him.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v8-table.text: One verb in three times, around your walk. Now: voy a la panadería (I am going to the bakery). The plan: voy a comprar pan (I am going to buy bread). Over: fui a la panadería (I went to the bakery). For places: ¿Dónde está…?, está cerca or lejos (estar, not ser), a la izquierda, a la derecha, and hay (there is, there are). The book keeps them.
strings.lesson.el-pueblo.v8-recap.text: You can now ask where a place is and if it is far, ask if there is something, and say where you are going, what you are going to do there and where you went.
